strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: scalable EEG representations/tokenization across channel configurations and tasks.
The proposed TFM-Tokenizer is a coherent combination of single-channel VQ-style discrete tokenization, STFT-based frequency modeling, raw-signal temporal modeling, and masked token prediction.
Evaluation spans four EEG datasets and includes strong recent baselines such as BIOT and LaBraM, with generally positive results and five-seed reporting.
Ablations on raw-only vs STFT-only vs joint modeling, masking strategy, vocabulary size, position embeddings, and masked token prediction help support some design choices.
The paper goes beyond headline accuracy by analyzing token utilization, class-token uniqueness, retrieval behavior, and qualitative token motifs.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method largely composes established ingredients, including STFT features, VQ-VAE tokenization, transformer encoders, and masked prediction. The paper does not fully clarify which technical component is fundamentally new beyond this integration for EEG.

Several central claims about scalability, generalization, and foundation-model usefulness are stronger than the evidence. The experiments are mostly single-dataset pretraining and fine-tuning; there is no convincing cross-dataset transfer, zero/few-shot evaluation, cross-device evaluation, or systematic missing-channel/few-channel study.

Reported gains are often modest and sometimes comparable to standard deviations, especially on TUEV and TUAB. The paper does not provide significance tests or confidence intervals to establish that improvements over BIOT/LaBraM are robust.

The token-quality analyses are not fully convincing. Class-token uniqueness can be confounded by vocabulary utilization and class imbalance, the Jaccard retrieval setup is only lightly specified, and applying Fourier/spectral entropy analysis directly to arbitrary discrete token IDs is questionable because token indices do not have inherent metric or frequency semantics.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility need more detail. The proposed model appears heavily tuned with Ray Tune, but it is unclear whether baselines received comparable tuning; code release is not stated; preprocessing, channel harmonization, and exact train/pretrain split handling are not sufficiently auditable.
Interpretability evidence is mostly qualitative, based on a few selected visual examples, and is not validated by clinicians or quantitative motif-consistency measures.

Some methodological exposition is dimensionally or conceptually unclear, for example the description of quantization along the time axis versus conventional VQ, the gated aggregation equations, and the precise construction of frequency patches and masks.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering TUEV, TUAB, IIIC-Seizure, CHB-MIT, and an ear-EEG sleep-staging transfer setting, with comparisons to strong recent EEG foundation models.

The results are generally strong: the method improves several key metrics, often with fewer parameters, and the plug-and-play experiments with BIOT and LaBraM support the claim that the tokenizer can benefit other backbones.

The paper includes useful ablations on temporal versus spectral inputs, masking strategies, vocabulary size, downstream depth, and positional embeddings, plus token-level analyses that help interpret what the tokenizer is learning.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: the core ingredients, including STFT features, VQ-style codebooks, masked reconstruction, and transformer encoders, are familiar; the paper's main contribution is their EEG-specific combination and validation.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, the method does not uniformly outperform all baselines on every metric, and several plug-and-play settings improve some metrics while degrading others such as balanced accuracy.

The fairness of comparisons is not fully settled. Some baselines are reproduced under reduced or modified pretraining settings, others use reported results or official weights, and the paper would benefit from a clearer accounting of pretraining data, test-set exclusion, and compute budgets.
The reproducibility statement and abstract appear to omit the actual code/model URL, which is a concrete reproducibility weakness despite the useful hyperparameter appendix.

Several token-quality analyses are suggestive but not fully rigorous. In particular, applying spectral entropy to discrete token sequences is hard to interpret because token IDs are arbitrary categorical labels, and the qualitative motif analysis is small-scale.

The cross-device scalability result is promising but limited: EESM23 has only 10 subjects, the improvement is modest in absolute terms, and the evaluation does not yet establish broad device-agnostic generalization.

The writing is mostly clear but has some formula and presentation ambiguities, especially around gated aggregation dimensions, token utilization/uniqueness definitions, and whether parameter counts include tokenizer components consistently.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: reusable EEG tokenization for foundation models, with a clear motivation for single-channel operation and cross-device flexibility.
The proposed architecture is reasonably coherent, combining temporal and time-frequency representations with VQ-style discrete codes and masked reconstruction/pretraining objectives.
The empirical scope is broader than many EEG papers, covering several public datasets, multiple baselines, ablations, integration with BIOT/LaBraM, and an ear-EEG transfer experiment.
weaknesses: The main contribution appears incremental relative to existing VQ tokenizers, masked EEG modeling, STFT-based EEG representations, and foundation-model preprocessing. The novelty claims, especially around motif tokenization, are stronger than what is technically established.

The evaluation has serious fairness and validity concerns. Some baselines are reproduced under reduced or altered pretraining regimes, others use reported numbers, and it is unclear whether multi-dataset self-supervised pretraining excludes target test data. Parameter counting is also inconsistent across tokenizers and downstream models.

Several headline claims overstate the evidence. The method does not dominate all metrics, e.g. CHB-MIT balanced accuracy is worse than BIOT in the multi-dataset setting, and many gains are small relative to standard deviations. Relative percentage improvements make modest absolute gains look larger.

The token-quality and interpretability analyses are weak. Class-token uniqueness and Jaccard retrieval are ad hoc, the qualitative motif figure is highly selective, and the spectral entropy analysis of token sequences is questionable because discrete code indices do not have an inherent frequency-domain ordering.

Ablations do not isolate several important design choices convincingly, such as VQ versus continuous embeddings, simple STFT tokenization, masking objectives, codebook collapse/perplexity, fixed-window artifacts, channel aggregation choices, and the effect of pretraining corpus size.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code/weights URL is blank, implementation details for some comparisons and statistical tests are underspecified, and the paper contains formatting, citation, and writing issues that reduce confidence in the experimental record.

The ear-EEG scalability result is based on a very small subject split and likely segment-level statistics; the claimed cross-device generalization is therefore suggestive but not yet convincing for a top-tier venue.
